In [[mathematics]], the '''Hjelmslev transformation''' is an effective method for [[Map (mathematics)|mapping]] an entire [[Hyperbolic space|hyperbolic plane]] into a [[circle]] with a finite [[radius]]. The transformation was invented by Danish mathematician [[Johannes Hjelmslev]]. It utilizes [[Nikolai Ivanovich Lobachevsky]]'s 23rd theorem<ref>"For every given angle a there is a line p such that Π(p) = a"</ref> from his work [[Geometrical Investigations on the Theory of Parallels]].

[[File:Hjemslev-mapping-example.png|thumb|The Hjelmslev transformation is a method of mapping an infinite line into a finite one in [[hyperbolic geometry]].]]

Lobachevsky observes, using a combination of his 16th and 23rd theorems, that it is a fundamental characteristic of [[hyperbolic geometry]] that there must exist a distinct [[angle of parallelism]] for any given line length.<ref>{{Cite book|last=Lobachevski|first=Nicholas|url=https://www.stmarys-ca.edu/sites/default/files/attachments/files/Theory_of_Parallels.pdf|title=Geometrical Researches on The Theory of Parallels|publisher=The Open Court Publishing Company|year=1914|location=Chicago, Illinois|pages=13–14 (Theorem 16), 19–21 (Theorem 23)}}</ref> Let us say for the length AE, its angle of parallelism is angle BAF. This being the case, line AH and EJ will be [[hyperbolic geometry|hyperparallel]], and therefore will never meet. Consequently, any line drawn perpendicular to base AE between A and E must necessarily cross line AH at some finite distance. [[Johannes Hjelmslev]] discovered from this a method of compressing an entire hyperbolic plane into a finite circle. 

== Construction ==

=== Formalisation ===
The Hjelmslev transformation is a function designated as <math>H(P)</math> which operates upon all points <math>P_n</math> in hyperbolic (Lobachevskian) space. Given an angle <math>\alpha</math> such that <math>0 < \alpha < \frac{\pi}{2}</math>, and an origin <math>O</math>, this mapping yields images <math>P'_n</math> where the following properties are preserved:

# The image of a circle with a center at <math>O</math> is a circle with a center at <math>O</math>.
# The image of a rectilinear angle is a rectilinear angle.
# Any angle with vertex <math>O</math> is mapped onto itself, i.e. any angle with vertex <math>O</math> is preserved.
# The image of a right angle with one side passing through <math>O</math> is a right angle with one side passing through <math>O</math>.
# The image of any straight line will be a finite straight line segment.
# Finally, the point order is maintained throughout a transformation, i.e. if B is between A and C, the image of B will be between the image of A and the image of C.

This function is useful in the studies of hyperbolic (Lobachevskian) space because it produces characteristic figures of parallel lines. Given a set of two parallel lines <math>\overline{AB}</math>, <math>\overline{CD}</math> such that <math>\overline{AB} \parallel \overline{CD}</math>, the resulting images <math>\overline{A'B'}</math>, <math>\overline{C'D'}</math> will form a triangle <math>\triangle A'B'IC'D'</math> with an imaginary vertex <math>I</math> in their direction of parallelism.

=== Transformation of a single point <math>P</math> into image <math>P'</math> ===

Given <math>\alpha</math>, <math>O</math>, <math>P</math>, in order to find the <math>P'</math> (image) of <math>P</math>. First draw the line segment <math>\overline{OP}</math>, connecting the point <math>P</math> to the origin <math>O</math>. Next, construct an auxiliary line <math>\overline{OQ}</math> such that <math>\angle POQ = \alpha</math>. Point <math>Q</math> is only necessary to define the line <math>\overline{OQ}</math>.

[[File:Line OQ at angle -alpha from OP.png|center|thumb|Line <math>\overline{OQ}</math> at angle <math>\alpha</math> from <math>\overline{OP}</math>.]]

Now construct the perpendicular line <math>\overline{PP''}
</math> passing through the point <math>P</math>, perpendicular to <math>\overline{OQ}</math>. This will form the right angle <math>\angle OP''P
</math> at point <math>P''</math>:

[[File:Perpendicular of line PP-double-prime onto line OQ..png|center|thumb|Perpendicular <math>\overline{PP''}</math> onto <math>\overline{OQ}</math>.]]

Using line segment <math>\overline{OP''}</math> as a radius, construct a circle with center <math>O</math> such that the circumference of said circle intersects <math>\overline{OP}</math> at a point <math>\color{red} P'</math>. Thus, we obtain the point <math>\color{red} P'</math> on line segment <math>OP</math>, which is the Hjelmslev transformation <math>H(P)</math> of the given point <math>P</math>. <math>H(P) = \color{red} P'</math>:

[[File:Point P-prime from radius OP-double-prime.png|center|thumb|Point <math>P'</math> from radius <math>\overline{OP''}</math>.]]

=== The Hjelmslev Disk ===
Let <math>\overline{P_1P_2}</math> be parallel to <math>\overline{P_3P_4}</math>, where <math>\angle P_3 P_1 P_2</math> is the angle of parallelism. By performing the transformation for every point on the two parallel lines, we yield the Hjelmslev circle:

[[File:Transformation of Parallel Lines P1 P2 and P3 P4.png|center|frameless]]

The circumference of the circle created does not have a corresponding location within the plane, and therefore, the product of a Hjelmslev transformation is more aptly called a '''Hjelmslev Disk'''. Likewise, when this transformation is extended in all three dimensions, it is referred to as a '''Hjelmslev Ball'''.

[[Image:Hjintersecting.svg|frame|left|A completed Hjelmslev disk representing two intersecting lines]]
[[Image:Hjparallel.svg|frame|left|A completed Hjelmslev disk representing two hyperparallel lines]]
[[Image:Hjultra.svg|frame|left|A completed Hjelmslev disk representing two ultraparallel lines]]

==The Hjelmslev transformation and the Klein model==
If we represent hyperbolic space by means of the [[Klein model]], and take the center of the Hjelmslev transformation to be the center point of the Klein model, then the Hjelmslev transformation maps points in the [[unit disk]] to points in a disk centered at the origin with a radius less than one. Given a [[real number]] k, the Hjelmslev transformation, if we ignore rotations, is in effect what we obtain by mapping a vector u representing a point in the Klein model to
ku, with 0<k<1. It is therefore in terms of the model a [[uniform scaling]] which sends lines to lines and so forth. To beings living in a hyperbolic space it might be a suitable way of making a map.
